q: A performance analyst has to work out the Net Tonne Kilometres per engine day of a railway which performed 52,00,000 Net Tonne Kilometres during a period in which the goods engine days numbered 1,300. The Net Tonne Kilometres per engine day work out to:
e: Net Tonne Kilometres per engine day is NTKM divided by goods engine days. Here it is 52,00,000 / 1,300 = 4,000.

q: A statistics clerk has to report the density of passenger traffic on a railway which performed 1,44,00,000 passenger kilometres during a year in which the route kilometres open for traffic were 4,800. The density of passenger traffic on the railway works out to:

options.A: 3,000 passenger kilometres per route kilometre
options.B: 2,500 passenger kilometres per route kilometre
options.C: 300 passenger kilometres per route kilometre
options.D: 30,000 passenger kilometres per route kilometre

e: Density of passenger traffic is passenger kilometres divided by route kilometres. Here it is 1,44,00,000 / 4,800 = 3,000 passenger kilometres per route kilometre.

q: During a period, the total wagon kilometres run on a railway were 80,00,000, of which the empty wagon kilometres were 32,00,000. The percentage of empty wagon kilometres to total wagon kilometres is:
e: Percentage of empty wagon kilometres is empty wagon kilometres divided by total wagon kilometres. Here it is 32,00,000 / 80,00,000 x 100 = 40 per cent.

q: The passenger earnings of a railway for a period are Rs 1,35,00,000 and the number of passengers carried during the period is 27,00,000. The earnings per passenger of the railway for the period are:

options.B: Rs 4
options.C: Rs 50
options.D: Rs 5

e: Earnings per passenger is passenger earnings divided by passengers carried. Here it is 1,35,00,000 / 27,00,000 = Rs 5.

q: The gross earnings of a railway for a period are Rs 3,00,00,000. During the same period it performed 60,00,000 passenger kilometres and 60,00,000 Net Tonne Kilometres. The earnings per traffic unit of the railway work out to:
e: Traffic units are 60,00,000 passenger kilometres plus 60,00,000 Net Tonne Kilometres = 1,20,00,000. Earnings per traffic unit = 3,00,00,000 / 1,20,00,000 = Rs 2.50.

q: A railway performed 96,00,000 passenger kilometres during a period in which the passenger train kilometres run were 16,000. The average number of passengers carried per train is:
e: Average passengers per train is passenger kilometres divided by passenger train kilometres. Here it is 96,00,000 / 16,000 = 600.

q: The coaching earnings of a railway for a period are Rs 96,00,000 and the coaching train kilometres run during the period are 1,20,000. The earnings per coaching train kilometre work out to:

options.A: Rs 8
options.B: Rs 80
options.C: Rs 800
options.D: Rs 40

e: Earnings per coaching train kilometre is coaching earnings divided by coaching train kilometres. Here it is 96,00,000 / 1,20,000 = Rs 80.

q: A traffic costing cell has worked out that the total cost of the goods services of a railway for a period is Rs 49,00,000 and the Net Tonne Kilometres performed are 14,00,000. The cost per Net Tonne Kilometre works out to:
e: Cost per Net Tonne Kilometre is total goods cost divided by NTKM. Here it is 49,00,000 / 14,00,000 = Rs 3.50.

q: During the internal check of a station's goods accounts, the Traffic Accounts Office finds that a consignor has been charged freight in excess of what was due on his consignment. For such an excess charge detected in check, the document prepared in the Traffic Accounts Office is the:

options.A: Overcharge sheet
options.B: Error sheet
options.C: Advice of Internal Check
options.D: Stock sheet

e: Where internal check in the Traffic Accounts Office detects that a consignor has been charged freight in excess of what was due, an overcharge sheet is prepared for refund of the excess.

q: A station has deposited its earnings at a focal point branch of the bank, and the traffic Cash Office has to afford credit for the remittance in its accounts. Credits for remittances deposited by stations at the focal point branches of the bank are afforded in the Cash Office on the basis of:

options.A: The Station Balance Sheet alone
options.B: The error sheets issued to the station
options.C: The scrolls/returns of remittances received from the bank
options.D: The oral confirmation of the Station Master

e: Credits for station remittances deposited at focal point bank branches are afforded in the traffic Cash Office on the basis of the scrolls or returns of remittances received from the bank.

q: A station which renders both coaching and goods accounts receives its Advice of Internal Check from the Traffic Accounts Office in two separate parts, one covering its coaching transactions and the other its goods transactions. This is because the Advice of Internal Check is prepared by the Traffic Accounts Office:

options.A: Only after the close of the financial year
options.B: Separately for coaching and for goods accounts, after check of the station balance sheet
options.C: By the Travelling Inspector of Accounts during his inspection
options.D: Only for stations which have outstandings at the end of the month

e: The Advice of Internal Check is prepared by the Traffic Accounts Office separately for coaching and for goods accounts after check of the station balance sheet, so a station rendering both accounts receives it in two parts.

q: At the close of the financial year, the balance under Traffic Suspense of a zonal railway stands on the debit side, the amount representing 'to-pay' freight and other traffic dues which have been taken into earnings but have not yet been realised from the parties. A debit balance under Traffic Suspense broadly indicates:

options.A: Refunds payable to passengers and merchants
options.B: Excess cash deposited by the stations of the railway
options.C: Profit earned by the Traffic Department during the year
options.D: Traffic dues/outstanding earnings yet to be recovered or adjusted

e: A debit balance under Traffic Suspense represents to-pay freight and other traffic dues taken into earnings but not yet realised, i.e. traffic outstandings yet to be recovered or adjusted.

q: A soldier travels by train on a military warrant issued by his unit and presents the warrant at the booking office. In regard to the ticket issued to him and the fare for the journey, the correct position is that:

options.A: A ticket is issued in exchange for the warrant, the fare being recovered from the department concerned
options.B: He travels free, and no accountal or recovery of the fare is made from anyone
options.C: He must pay the fare in cash, the warrant being only an identity document
options.D: A ticket is issued only at the destination station, after the journey is over

e: On a military warrant, a ticket is issued in exchange for the warrant and the fare is recovered from the department concerned, not paid in cash by the soldier.

q: A consignor loads and packs his goods himself and the railway staff do not check the contents of the packages, the Railway Receipt being endorsed 'said to contain'. This endorsement on the Railway Receipt signifies that:

options.A: The consignment is booked at railway risk in all respects
options.B: The goods were packed and loaded by the consignor and their contents were not checked by the railway staff
options.C: The freight on the consignment has not been paid by the consignor
options.D: The consignment consists of perishable goods requiring speedy despatch

e: The endorsement said to contain on a Railway Receipt signifies that the goods were packed and loaded by the consignor and their contents were not checked by the railway staff.

q: At a forwarding station, the loading of a consignment into the wagon is performed by railway labour engaged for the purpose, instead of by the consignor's own labour. In regard to the charges for such handling, the correct position is that:

options.A: The handling is done free of charge in all cases
options.B: The charges are borne by the destination station out of its earnings
options.C: Handling charges are recovered from the consignor or the consignee, as the case may be, in addition to the freight
options.D: The charges are shared equally between the Railways and the party in all cases

e: Where loading at the forwarding station is performed by railway labour instead of the consignor's labour, handling charges are recovered from the consignor or consignee, as the case may be, in addition to freight.

q: A passenger questions why the fare for his journey has been computed over the longer route by which his train actually runs, instead of over the shortest road distance between the two stations. Passenger fares for a train journey are charged on the basis of:

options.A: The shortest road distance between the two stations
options.B: The straight-line distance between the two stations
options.C: A uniform distance slab for all trains on the section
options.D: The distance by the route by which the train actually travels

e: Passenger fares are charged on the distance by the route by which the train actually travels, not on the shortest road or straight-line distance.

q: The statistical organisation of a railway has to compile the passenger kilometres performed during a month, covering both reserved and unreserved travel. For compiling the passenger statistics, the passenger kilometres are worked out:

options.A: From the tickets issued, by multiplying the number of passengers with the distance of the journey in each case
options.B: From the reservation charts of the reserved trains only
options.C: From the statements rendered by the guards of the trains
options.D: By estimation, without reference to the tickets issued

e: Passenger kilometres are compiled from the tickets issued, by multiplying the number of passengers by the distance of journey in each case, covering both reserved and unreserved travel.

q: In the coaching stock return of a railway, a number of coaches are shown apart from the coaches available for traffic, as they are undergoing repairs in the workshop or are awaiting repairs. Coaching vehicles which are under repair or awaiting repair and are not available for traffic use are termed:

options.A: Effective stock
options.B: Ineffective stock
options.C: Surplus stock
options.D: Departmental stock

e: Coaching vehicles under repair or awaiting repair and not available for traffic use are termed ineffective stock, as distinct from effective stock available for service.

q: A coaching statistics clerk is computing the vehicle days of his railway for a month and asks what a 'vehicle day' means for this purpose. In coaching statistics, a 'vehicle day' means:

options.A: One coaching vehicle under repair for a period of 24 hours
options.B: One vehicle run for a distance of 100 kilometres
options.C: One coaching vehicle on line (available) for a period of 24 hours
options.D: One coach carrying passengers during a calendar day

e: In coaching statistics, a vehicle day means one coaching vehicle on line (available) for a period of 24 hours.

q: At a junction station, the staff record every wagon and vehicle handed over to, and received from, the neighbouring zonal railway. These interchange records maintained at junction points form the basis of:

options.A: The pay bills of the junction staff
options.B: The classification of goods for the purpose of freight rating
options.C: The fixation of passenger fares from the junction station
options.D: Wagon-usage and interchange statistics between the railways

e: Interchange records of wagons and vehicles handed over and received at junction points between railways form the basis of wagon-usage and interchange statistics.

q: A loco foreman's return shows a locomotive running by itself from the shed to the station to take charge of a train, without hauling any load on that run. In railway statistics, such engine kilometres run by a locomotive without hauling any train or load are known as:

options.A: Light engine kilometres
options.B: Shunting kilometres
options.C: Train kilometres
options.D: Coaching kilometres

e: Engine kilometres run by a locomotive by itself, without hauling any train or load, such as from shed to station, are light engine kilometres.

q: A statistics clerk, while compiling the monthly operating returns, adds the shunting kilometres performed in the yards to the train kilometres of the railway. The correct position in this regard is that:

options.A: Shunting kilometres are included in train kilometres, but not in engine kilometres
options.B: Shunting kilometres are included in engine kilometres, but they are not included in train kilometres
options.C: Shunting kilometres are excluded from both engine kilometres and train kilometres
options.D: Shunting kilometres are counted as coaching kilometres of the railway

e: Shunting kilometres performed in yards are included in engine kilometres, since the engine is working, but they are not included in train kilometres, since no train is run.

q: A safety review of a zonal railway has to compare its safety performance with that of other railways, using the index commonly adopted for the purpose. The safety performance of a railway is commonly measured by the index of:

options.A: Train accidents per route kilometre
options.B: Train accidents per passenger carried
options.C: Train accidents per million train kilometres
options.D: Engine failures per lakh engine kilometres

e: Safety performance of a railway is commonly measured by the index of train accidents per million train kilometres, which allows comparison between railways of different sizes.

q: The Railway Board calls for the periodical telegraphic report of approximate gross earnings of a zonal railway well before the accounts of the period are closed and apportioned. The periodical telegraphic report of approximate gross earnings of a zonal railway is compiled on:

options.A: Apportioned basis
options.B: Carried basis
options.C: Terminal basis
options.D: Originating basis

e: The periodical telegraphic report of approximate gross earnings is compiled on the originating basis, i.e. earnings originating on the railway, before accounts are closed and apportioned.

q: An accounts officer has to trace the earnings of the local and through traffic of his zonal railway as shown in the Traffic Book. The Traffic Book of a zonal railway, showing the earnings of local and through traffic, is compiled in:

options.A: The Traffic Accounts Office of the railway
options.B: The Railway Board
options.C: The Commercial Department of the division
options.D: The Statistics cell of the Railway Board

e: The Traffic Book, showing earnings of local and through traffic of a zonal railway, is compiled in the Traffic Accounts Office of the railway.

q: A consignor books live animals for carriage by rail and engages his own attendant to accompany them in transit. During the journey, the responsibility for feeding and watering the animals rests with:

options.A: The guard of the train carrying the animals
options.B: The station staff at the destination station
options.C: The attendant deputed by the consignor, who accompanies the animals
options.D: The Traffic Accounts Office

e: For live animals booked by rail, feeding and watering in transit is the responsibility of the attendant deputed by the consignor who accompanies the animals.

q: Before accepting a consignment for carriage, the goods clerk insists that every package of the consignment be distinctly marked and labelled by the consignor. The Railways require this before a consignment is accepted for carriage so that:

options.A: The consignment can be insured by the consignor against all risks
options.B: The consignment can be identified and delivered correctly at the destination
options.C: The consignment can be weighed at the consignor's own premises
options.D: The packages can be packed only in wooden cases

e: Every package must be distinctly marked and labelled by the consignor before acceptance so that the consignment can be identified and delivered correctly at the destination.

q: The operating department has imposed restrictions on the booking of goods traffic to a terminal which has become congested, and the restrictions have been notified to all stations. A forwarding station which has received the notification is required:

options.A: To continue booking such traffic, charging double freight on it
options.B: To send the traffic by road at railway cost
options.C: To book the traffic only for stations short of the congested terminal
options.D: Not to accept booking of traffic in contravention of the restrictions in force

e: A forwarding station that has received notification of booking restrictions for a congested terminal must not accept booking of traffic in contravention of the restrictions in force.

q: A passenger holding a confirmed reserved ticket discontinues his journey midway of his own accord and claims refund of the fare for the untravelled portion of the journey. In regard to such a claim, the correct position is that he is:

options.A: Ordinarily not entitled to any refund for the untravelled portion
options.B: Entitled to a full refund of the fare for the untravelled portion
options.C: Entitled to a free ticket for the return journey
options.D: Entitled to a refund of fare less only the reservation charge

e: A passenger who discontinues his journey midway of his own accord is ordinarily not entitled to any refund of fare for the untravelled portion.

q: A passenger holding a waitlisted ticket issued at a computerised reservation counter, that is, a paper ticket, boards the train and seeks to travel in the reserved coach. In regard to such a waitlisted paper ticket, the correct position is that the passenger is:

options.A: Treated as travelling without a ticket if he boards the train
options.B: Permitted to board and travel in the reserved coach of the train
options.C: Not permitted to enter the reserved coach of the train
options.D: Required to surrender the ticket at the station before the train departs

e: A waitlisted paper (PRS counter) ticket does not entitle the holder to enter or travel in a reserved coach; unlike an e-ticket it is not auto-cancelled, but reserved-coach travel on it is not permitted - the passenger may travel only in unreserved accommodation (Answer: C).

q: A divisional officer assessing the punctuality performance of the passenger trains of his division is advised to judge it primarily by one criterion. The punctuality performance of passenger trains is assessed primarily with reference to:

options.A: Their right-time departure from the originating stations
options.B: The number of trains run during the period
options.C: Their right-time arrival at the destination station
options.D: The average speed attained by them over the section

e: Punctuality of passenger trains is assessed primarily with reference to their right-time arrival at the destination station.

q: A booking clerk charges the same reservation charge on a Sleeper class ticket and on an AC class ticket, and the passenger questions the charge. The correct position regarding the reservation charge levied on a reserved ticket is that it:

options.A: Is uniform for all classes of travel
options.B: Is levied only on tickets in the air-conditioned classes
options.C: Is levied only on Tatkal tickets
options.D: Varies according to the class of travel

e: The reservation charge on a reserved ticket is prescribed class-wise and varies according to the class of travel; it is not a uniform charge for all classes.

q: A goods clerk has to charge freight on a consignment presented for booking, the consignor's declared weight differing from the weight found at the station. Freight on a goods consignment is normally charged on the basis of:

options.A: The weight ascertained by weighment of the consignment at the forwarding station
options.B: The weight declared by the consignor, which is never verified by the Railways
options.C: The volumetric measurement of the packages in all cases
options.D: A flat charge per wagon, irrespective of the weight loaded

e: Freight on a goods consignment is normally charged on the weight ascertained by weighment of the consignment at the forwarding station, not merely on the consignor's declared weight.

q: An operating officer uses the index 'Gross Tonne Kilometres per engine day' to judge the performance of the locomotive fleet of his railway. This index measures:

options.A: The fuel efficiency of the locomotives of the railway
options.B: The gross hauling output obtained per locomotive day
options.C: The utilisation of wagons in terms of the distance run by them
options.D: The occupation of the line by trains during the day

e: Gross Tonne Kilometres per engine day measures the gross hauling output obtained per locomotive day, i.e. the work done by the locomotive fleet.

q: An accounts officer needs, for a review, the gross earnings of his railway for a month as finally brought to account, and not the approximate figures compiled for the ten-day periods. The monthly gross earnings of a railway as finally brought to account are shown in:

options.A: Statement 6A
options.B: Statement 2
options.C: Statement 7C
options.D: Statement 7A

e: The monthly gross earnings of a railway as finally brought to account, as distinct from the approximate ten-day figures, are shown in Statement 7A of the Traffic Book.

q: A station accountant is closing the monthly Station Balance Sheet. The opening outstanding balance of the month was Rs 5,10,000, the earnings and other debits of the month were Rs 18,20,000, and the remittances and other credits of the month were Rs 19,60,000. The closing outstanding balance of the month works out to:
e: Closing outstanding equals opening outstanding plus debits minus credits: 5,10,000 + 18,20,000 - 19,60,000 = Rs 3,70,000.

q: The statistical cell of a zonal railway has to report the total track kilometres of a section whose route length is 90 kilometres, laid with two running lines throughout, and which has, in addition, 28 kilometres of sidings, yard lines and other tracks. Counting each line separately, as track kilometres are counted, the total track kilometres of the section work out to:

options.A: 90 kilometres
options.B: 118 kilometres
options.C: 180 kilometres
options.D: 208 kilometres

e: Track kilometres count each running line separately, plus sidings and yard lines. Here it is 90 x 2 + 28 = 208 kilometres.

q: A costing officer is verifying a loco shed's monthly return, which shows that the goods locomotives consumed 7,200 litres of diesel oil during the month while performing 16,00,000 Gross Tonne Kilometres. On verification, the Specific Fuel Consumption (SFC) of the railway for the month works out to:

options.A: 0.45 litres per 1000 GTKM
options.B: 45.0 litres per 1000 GTKM
options.C: 4.5 litres per 1000 GTKM
options.D: 2.2 litres per 1000 GTKM

e: Specific Fuel Consumption is fuel per 1000 GTKM. Here it is 7,200 / (16,00,000 / 1000) = 7,200 / 1,600 = 4.5 litres per 1000 GTKM.

q: During a month, the locomotives in electric traction on a railway consumed 96,000 kWh of electrical energy and performed 40,00,000 Gross Tonne Kilometres. The Specific Energy Consumption (SEC) of the railway for the month works out to:

options.A: 24 kWh per 1000 Gross Tonne Kilometres
options.B: 2.4 kWh per 1000 Gross Tonne Kilometres
options.C: 240 kWh per 1000 Gross Tonne Kilometres
options.D: 42 kWh per 1000 Gross Tonne Kilometres

e: Specific Energy Consumption is energy per 1000 GTKM. Here it is 96,000 / (40,00,000 / 1000) = 96,000 / 4,000 = 24 kWh per 1000 GTKM.

q: At an occupancy review, a division reports that against 75,00,000 seat kilometres offered during the period, its coaching services actually performed 48,00,000 passenger kilometres. The load factor (occupation ratio) reported for the coaching services is:
e: Load factor is passenger kilometres divided by seat kilometres offered. Here it is 48,00,000 / 75,00,000 x 100 = 64 per cent.

q: A finance officer is reviewing the annual results of a zonal railway whose gross earnings for the year are Rs 4,000 crore and whose working expenses are Rs 3,720 crore. The Operating Ratio of the railway for the year works out to:
e: Operating Ratio is working expenses as a percentage of gross earnings. Here it is 3720 / 4000 x 100 = 93 per cent.

q: A statistics clerk is closing the monthly wagon performance return of a railway. During the month, the total wagon days on the railway were 10,20,000 and the number of wagons loaded was 3,40,000. The wagon turn-round for the month works out to:

options.A: 3.4 days
options.B: 4.0 days
options.C: 3.0 days
options.D: 2.5 days

e: Wagon turn-round is wagon days divided by wagons loaded. Here it is 10,20,000 / 3,40,000 = 3.0 days.

q: A costing officer has to work out the average lead of the goods traffic of a railway which performed 1,82,00,000 Net Tonne Kilometres during a period in which the tonnes carried were 2,60,000. The average lead of goods traffic of the railway works out to:

options.A: 70 km
options.B: 60 km
options.C: 65 km
options.D: 80 km

e: Average lead of goods traffic is Net Tonne Kilometres divided by tonnes carried. Here it is 1,82,00,000 / 2,60,000 = 70 km.

q: A traffic costing cell has worked out that the total cost of the coaching services of a railway for a period is Rs 84,00,000 and the passenger kilometres performed are 1,40,00,000. The cost per passenger kilometre works out to:
e: Cost per passenger kilometre is total coaching cost divided by passenger kilometres. Here it is 84,00,000 / 1,40,00,000 = Rs 0.60.

q: A loco foreman is checking a monthly return which shows that the locomotives of a railway ran 15,60,000 engine kilometres during the month and the engine days numbered 3,900. The engine kilometres per engine day work out to:
e: Engine kilometres per engine day is engine kilometres divided by engine days. Here it is 15,60,000 / 3,900 = 400.

q: A performance analyst has to work out the Net Tonne Kilometres per engine day of a railway which performed 63,00,000 Net Tonne Kilometres during a period in which the goods engine days numbered 1,400. The Net Tonne Kilometres per engine day work out to:
e: Net Tonne Kilometres per engine day is NTKM divided by goods engine days. Here it is 63,00,000 / 1,400 = 4,500.

q: A statistics clerk has to report the density of passenger traffic on a railway which performed 1,75,00,000 passenger kilometres during a year in which the route kilometres open for traffic were 5,000. The density of passenger traffic on the railway works out to:

options.A: 3,500 passenger kilometres per route kilometre
options.B: 3,000 passenger kilometres per route kilometre
options.C: 350 passenger kilometres per route kilometre
options.D: 35,000 passenger kilometres per route kilometre

e: Density of passenger traffic is passenger kilometres divided by route kilometres. Here it is 1,75,00,000 / 5,000 = 3,500 passenger kilometres per route kilometre.

q: During a period, the total wagon kilometres run on a railway were 90,00,000, of which the empty wagon kilometres were 27,00,000. The percentage of empty wagon kilometres to total wagon kilometres is:
e: Percentage of empty wagon kilometres is empty wagon kilometres divided by total wagon kilometres. Here it is 27,00,000 / 90,00,000 x 100 = 30 per cent.

q: A traffic costing cell has worked out that the total cost of the goods services of a railway for a period is Rs 60,00,000 and the Net Tonne Kilometres performed are 15,00,000. The cost per Net Tonne Kilometre works out to:
e: Cost per Net Tonne Kilometre is total goods cost divided by NTKM. Here it is 60,00,000 / 15,00,000 = Rs 4.00.

q: The passenger earnings of a railway for a period are Rs 1,68,00,000 and the number of passengers carried during the period is 28,00,000. The earnings per passenger of the railway for the period are:

options.B: Rs 5
options.C: Rs 6
options.D: Rs 60

e: Earnings per passenger is passenger earnings divided by passengers carried. Here it is 1,68,00,000 / 28,00,000 = Rs 6.

q: The gross earnings of a railway for a period are Rs 3,60,00,000. During the same period it performed 80,00,000 passenger kilometres and 40,00,000 Net Tonne Kilometres. The earnings per traffic unit of the railway work out to:
e: Earnings per traffic unit equal gross earnings divided by total traffic units, where one passenger kilometre and one Net Tonne Kilometre each count as one unit. Here Rs 3,60,00,000 divided by (80,00,000 + 40,00,000) = Rs 3,60,00,000 / 1,20,00,000 = Rs 3.00.

q: A performance analyst has to work out the Net Tonne Kilometres per wagon day of a railway which performed 24,50,000 Net Tonne Kilometres during a period in which the wagon days numbered 70,000. The Net Tonne Kilometres per wagon day work out to:
e: Net Tonne Kilometres per wagon day equal Net Tonne Kilometres divided by wagon days. Here 24,50,000 / 70,000 = 35, which measures the average revenue load moved per wagon per day.

q: The Net Tonne Kilometres performed on a railway are 6,00,00,000 and the loaded wagon kilometres are 15,00,000. The average load of a loaded wagon on the railway works out to:

options.A: 35 tonnes
options.B: 40 tonnes
options.C: 45 tonnes
options.D: 30 tonnes

e: Average load of a loaded wagon equals Net Tonne Kilometres divided by loaded wagon kilometres. Here 6,00,00,000 / 15,00,000 = 40 tonnes.

q: The Gross Tonne Kilometres performed on a railway during a period are 1,80,00,000 and the goods train kilometres run are 50,000. The average gross load of goods trains on the railway works out to:

options.A: 300 tonnes
options.B: 400 tonnes
options.C: 360 tonnes
options.D: 180 tonnes

e: Average gross load of goods trains equals Gross Tonne Kilometres divided by goods train kilometres. Here 1,80,00,000 / 50,000 = 360 tonnes.

q: A railway performed 1,12,00,000 passenger kilometres during a period in which the passenger train kilometres run were 16,000. The average number of passengers carried per train on the railway works out to:
e: Average passengers per train equal passenger kilometres divided by passenger train kilometres. Here 1,12,00,000 / 16,000 = 700 passengers per train.

q: A merchant who has booked goods at a forwarding station asks the goods clerk what the Railway Receipt given to him stands for in law. The correct answer is that a Railway Receipt is:

options.A: A mere cash memo issued at the goods shed for the freight collected
options.B: A receipt for the goods accepted for carriage and evidence of the contract of carriage
options.C: A voucher on which the merchant can claim refund of freight
options.D: A document issued only in respect of parcel traffic

e: Under the Railways Act and Commercial Manual, a Railway Receipt is the receipt for goods accepted for carriage and evidence of the contract of carriage, to be surrendered for delivery.

q: At the close of a month, the goods clerk of a station has still to collect the freight on a number of consignments which were booked on a 'to-pay' basis and have been delivered. In the station accounts, this uncollected amount is shown as:

options.A: Freight already collected in cash and remitted to the bank
options.B: Freight deposited in advance by merchants for future bookings
options.C: Refund of freight payable to merchants by the station
options.D: Outstanding freight, being 'to-pay' freight on goods traffic which has not yet been collected

e: To-pay freight on delivered consignments not yet collected remains due to the Railways and is carried in station accounts as outstanding freight under goods outstandings.

q: A batch of concession vouchers and concession order forms comes up for check in the Traffic Accounts Office along with the accounts of a station. The check exercised on these vouchers is mainly to ensure that:

options.A: The concession was granted only to persons entitled to it and under proper authority
options.B: The vouchers are printed on good quality paper
options.C: A concession has been claimed by every passenger of the station
options.D: The highest fare has been charged in every case covered by a voucher

e: Traffic Accounts check of concession vouchers verifies that the concession was allowed only to entitled persons and under proper authority, so no unauthorised fare reduction escapes accountal.

q: A passenger at a small station asks for a ticket to a destination for which the printed card ticket of the class he wants is not available in the station's stock. In such a case, the booking clerk issues to him a:

options.A: Duplicate ticket in place of the ticket he has lost
options.B: Free pass for the journey, the fare being recovered later
options.C: Blank Paper Ticket, the printed card ticket for the required class and destination not being available in stock
options.D: Platform ticket endorsed for travel in the train

e: When the printed card ticket for the required class and destination is not in stock, the booking clerk issues a Blank Paper Ticket duly filled in for the journey.

q: During the check of a station's accounts in the Traffic Accounts Office, it is found that a number of tickets issued by the station have not been accounted for at all in the accounts rendered by it. In regard to the value of these unaccounted tickets, the Traffic Accounts Office:

options.A: Ignores the omission until the annual inspection of the station
options.B: Raises a debit against the station for the value of the unaccounted tickets
options.C: Cancels the entire remaining ticket stock of the station
options.D: Recovers the amount from the passengers to whom the tickets were sold

e: Tickets issued but omitted from the station accounts are debited by the Traffic Accounts Office against the station for their value, which the station must clear by accountal or payment.

q: A newly posted clerk at a station sees the expression 'coaching outstandings' in the station returns and asks what it broadly represents. The correct answer is that coaching outstandings broadly represent:

options.A: The cash held in the station safe at the close of the day
options.B: The refunds payable to passengers at the station
options.C: The salary dues of the booking staff of the station
options.D: The value of tickets and Excess Fare Tickets issued but not accounted for or remitted, recoverable from the station

e: Coaching outstandings broadly represent the value of tickets and Excess Fare Tickets issued but not accounted for or remitted, recoverable from the station.

q: At the end of a month, the Commercial and Accounts departments of a zonal railway sit together to reconcile the earnings figures maintained by the two departments. This monthly reconciliation of earnings is carried out primarily to:

options.A: Agree the statistical (approximate) earnings with the earnings actually brought to account and to investigate the differences
options.B: Fix the earnings targets of the railway for the next month
options.C: Allot rakes and wagons among the divisions of the railway
options.D: Decide the postings of the commercial staff of the railway

e: Monthly reconciliation agrees the Commercial Department approximate statistical earnings with the earnings actually brought to account by Accounts, and differences are investigated and cleared.

q: A statistics clerk of a zonal railway has to compile the monthly statistical statements of his railway. The material from which these statistical statements are compiled mainly consists of:

options.A: The reports published in newspapers about the working of the railway
options.B: The Budget documents of the Railway Board
options.C: The returns and statements rendered by the stations and operating units
options.D: The inspection reports of the audit department

e: Monthly statistical statements are compiled mainly from the returns and statements rendered by stations and operating units, which are the primary source records of traffic and operations.

q: A passenger travelling on a long through journey points out that his through fare works out to less than the sum of the fares for the separate parts of the journey. This is because passenger fares for through journeys are charged on the 'telescopic' principle, which means that:

options.A: The fare is the sum of the separate fares for each railway over which the journey is performed
options.B: The rate per kilometre decreases as the distance of the journey increases, so that the through fare is less than the sum of the fares for its parts
options.C: A flat fare is charged irrespective of the distance travelled
options.D: The fare increases in direct proportion to the square of the distance

e: Telescopic fares mean the rate per kilometre tapers as distance increases, so a through fare is less than the sum of separate fares for its parts.

q: At a forwarding station where no weighbridge is available, a consignor's declared weight is accepted for booking a consignment and the Railway Receipt is endorsed 'sender's weight accepted'. This endorsement indicates that:

options.A: The consignment was weighed on the railway weighbridge at the forwarding station
options.B: The overloading charges on the consignment have been accepted by the sender
options.C: The weight of the consignment can never be questioned thereafter
options.D: The weight declared by the consignor has been accepted for booking as no weighbridge is available at the forwarding station, subject to weighment en route or at destination

e: Sender's weight accepted means the consignor's declared weight is accepted for booking where no weighbridge exists at the forwarding station, subject to check weighment en route or at destination.

q: A newly posted accounts officer has to address a letter to the head of the Traffic Accounts Office of his zonal railway and asks under whose overall control that office functions. The correct answer is that the Traffic Accounts Office of a zonal railway functions under the overall control of the:

options.A: Financial Adviser and Chief Accounts Officer (FA & CAO) of the railway
options.B: General Manager of the railway, acting directly
options.C: Divisional Railway Manager of the division concerned
options.D: Railway Board, without reference to the zonal administration

e: The Traffic Accounts Office of a zonal railway functions under the overall control of the Financial Adviser and Chief Accounts Officer (FA and CAO) of that railway.

q: A passenger who has booked an e-ticket objects to the convenience fee collected from him, saying that it must be an earning of the Railways. The correct position regarding the convenience fee (service charge) levied by IRCTC on e-tickets is that it is:

options.A: An earning of the Railways, remitted by IRCTC to the Railways every month
options.B: Retained by IRCTC and does not form part of the earnings of the Railways
options.C: Shared equally between IRCTC and the Railways
options.D: Credited to the Traffic Suspense of the Railways

e: The convenience fee or service charge on e-tickets is levied and retained by IRCTC for its services and does not form part of railway earnings.

q: A traffic costing officer, while analysing the cost of a goods service, separates the costs incurred in loading, unloading and documentation at the two ends of the journey from the cost of hauling the traffic between them. The costs so separated at the originating and destination terminals are known, in traffic costing, as:

options.A: Terminal cost
options.B: The cost of constructing terminal stations
options.C: Line haul cost
options.D: Interest on capital invested in terminal facilities

e: In traffic costing, costs incurred at the originating and destination ends for loading, unloading and documentation are terminal costs, distinct from line haul cost of movement.

q: A customs officer posted away from any seaport clears export and import containers at a CONCOR facility in the interior of the country, and a freight customer asks what such a facility is. Inland Container Depots (ICDs) operated by CONCOR are:

options.A: Ports located on the sea coast for handling container ships
options.B: Depots for storing railway stores and materials
options.C: Dry ports where export/import containers are handled and customs formalities are completed away from the seaports
options.D: Terminals meant exclusively for parcel traffic

e: Inland Container Depots of CONCOR are dry ports in the interior where export and import containers are handled and customs clearance is completed away from seaports.

q: Certain amounts debited to a station on account of errors and deficiencies in its accounts are traced, on enquiry, to the mistakes of particular members of the station staff. The correct position regarding such debited amounts is that they are ultimately:

options.A: Borne by the Railways as a normal loss in all cases
options.B: Adjusted against the sundry earnings of the station
options.C: Recovered from the passengers and merchants concerned
options.D: Recoverable from the members of the station staff found responsible for the error or deficiency

e: Debits for errors and deficiencies traced to individual staff are ultimately recoverable from the members of station staff found responsible for the error or deficiency.

q: A batch of Parcel Way Bills rendered by a station comes up for check in the Traffic Accounts Office. This check is exercised primarily to ensure that:

options.A: The parcels were delivered on the very day of their arrival
options.B: The parcel vans were utilised to their full capacity
options.C: The parcel charges have been correctly levied in accordance with the scales in force and duly brought to account
options.D: The parcels were carried only by Rajdhani trains

e: Check of Parcel Way Bills in Traffic Accounts ensures parcel charges have been correctly levied as per scales in force and duly brought to account.

q: The goods invoices rendered by a forwarding station come up for check in the Traffic Accounts Office. The check is exercised with a view to verifying, among other things:

options.A: The correctness of the classification, chargeable weight and freight charged on the consignments
options.B: The handwriting of the goods clerks of the station
options.C: The punctuality of the goods trains dealt with at the station
options.D: The physical condition of the goods shed of the station

e: Check of goods invoices verifies correctness of classification, chargeable weight and freight charged, so undercharges and overcharges are detected and adjusted.

q: A station master has to explain to an auditor what the 'handling bills' rendered by his station relate to. The correct explanation is that handling bills relate to:

options.A: Bills for the pay and allowances of goods shed staff
options.B: Payments claimed by contractors engaged for handling, loading and unloading of goods and parcels at stations
options.C: Bills for the printing of goods invoices at the station
options.D: Claims of merchants for goods damaged at the station

e: Handling bills are claims of contractors engaged for handling, loading and unloading of goods and parcels at stations for payment of their handling charges.

q: In the Traffic Accounts Office, the outward returns of forwarding stations are tallied with the inward returns of destination stations. This tallying is done primarily to ensure that:

options.A: Wagons are allotted equitably among the stations
options.B: The tariffs in use at the stations are printed correctly
options.C: The staff posted at the stations are correctly shown in the returns
options.D: All traffic booked is duly accounted for and no consignment or freight escapes accountal

e: Tallying outward returns of forwarding stations with inward returns of destination stations ensures all traffic booked is duly accounted for and no consignment or freight escapes accountal.

q: A merchant who wants wagons for loading his goods at a station registers his demand for the wagons at the station. In goods traffic, the demand so registered by the consignor for supply of wagons is known as an:

options.A: Forwarding Note
options.B: Risk Note
options.C: Indent
options.D: Placement memo

e: A demand registered by a consignor at a station for supply of wagons for loading his goods is called an indent in goods traffic.

q: A consignee holding an electronic Railway Receipt under the Freight Operations Information System wants to take delivery of his consignment without visiting the Traffic Accounts Office. He can take delivery by:

options.A: Surrendering a hand-written copy of the receipt at the goods shed
options.B: Using the e-surrender facility, by which the electronic Railway Receipt is surrendered online for delivery
options.C: Applying to the Traffic Accounts Office for a delivery order
options.D: Obtaining an order of the Railway Claims Tribunal

e: Under FOIS, the holder of an electronic Railway Receipt can use the e-surrender facility to surrender it online and take delivery without visiting the Traffic Accounts Office.

q: A station master objects that the Traffic Accounts Office is checking his station's accounts long after the transactions took place and the accounts were rendered by him. This is because the check exercised by the Traffic Accounts Office over station accounts is a 'post-check', which means that it is:

options.A: Exercised before the transactions take place at the stations
options.B: Exercised by the statutory audit party after one year
options.C: Exercised only after the close of the financial year
options.D: Exercised after the transactions have taken place and the accounts have been rendered by the stations

e: Post-check means the Traffic Accounts check is exercised after transactions have taken place and station accounts have been rendered, not before the transactions.

q: A commercial officer studying the traffic pattern of his railway consults the 'passenger classification' statistics compiled on the Railways. These statistics show:

options.A: The number of passengers booked and the earnings, class-wise
options.B: The classification of trains as Mail, Express and Passenger
options.C: The classification of staff employed on passenger trains
options.D: The commodity classification of luggage traffic

e: Passenger classification statistics show the number of passengers booked and the earnings class-wise, for each class of travel.

q: A loco superintendent watches the 'percentage of engines under and awaiting repair' of his railway from month to month to judge the working of his organisation. This percentage is an index of:

options.A: The fuel efficiency of the locomotives of the railway
options.B: The utilisation of wagons on the railway
options.C: The repair position of locomotives and the efficiency of the locomotive maintenance organisation
options.D: The occupation of the line by trains during the day

e: Percentage of engines under and awaiting repair indicates the repair position of locomotives and the efficiency of the locomotive maintenance organisation.

q: A costing analyst finds that on his railway the Net Tonne Kilometres are a high proportion of the Gross Tonne Kilometres performed. The ratio of Net Tonne Kilometres to Gross Tonne Kilometres indicates:

options.A: The speed of goods trains on the railway
options.B: The proportion of the total load hauled which is revenue-earning (paying) load
options.C: The density of traffic on the line
options.D: The proportion of empty wagons in the wagon fleet

e: The ratio of Net Tonne Kilometres to Gross Tonne Kilometres shows the proportion of total hauled load that is revenue-earning paying load, the balance being tare weight.

q: A station accountant is closing the monthly Station Balance Sheet. The opening outstanding balance of the month was Rs 6,40,000, the earnings and other debits of the month were Rs 21,50,000, and the remittances and other credits of the month were Rs 24,10,000. The closing outstanding balance of the month works out to:
e: Closing outstanding equals opening outstanding plus debits minus credits. Here Rs 6,40,000 + Rs 21,50,000 - Rs 24,10,000 = Rs 3,80,000.

q: The statistical cell of a zonal railway has to report the total track kilometres of a section whose route length is 75 kilometres, laid with two running lines throughout, and which has, in addition, 32 kilometres of sidings, yard lines and other tracks. Counting each line separately, as track kilometres are counted, the total track kilometres of the section work out to:

options.A: 75 kilometres
options.B: 107 kilometres
options.C: 150 kilometres
options.D: 182 kilometres

e: Track kilometres count each line separately. Here running lines give 75 x 2 = 150 km, plus 32 km of sidings and other tracks = 182 km.

q: A costing officer is verifying a loco shed's monthly return, which shows that the goods locomotives consumed 9,900 litres of diesel oil during the month while performing 18,00,000 Gross Tonne Kilometres. On verification, the Specific Fuel Consumption (SFC) of the railway for the month works out to:

options.A: 0.55 litres per 1000 GTKM
options.B: 55.0 litres per 1000 GTKM
options.C: 5.5 litres per 1000 GTKM
options.D: 1.8 litres per 1000 GTKM

e: Specific Fuel Consumption equals fuel consumed divided by Gross Tonne Kilometres, expressed per 1000 GTKM. Here 9,900 / 18,00,000 x 1000 = 5.5 litres per 1000 GTKM.

q: During a month, the locomotives in electric traction on a railway consumed 88,000 kWh of electrical energy and performed 40,00,000 Gross Tonne Kilometres. The Specific Energy Consumption (SEC) of the railway for the month works out to:

options.A: 22 kWh per 1000 Gross Tonne Kilometres
options.B: 2.2 kWh per 1000 Gross Tonne Kilometres
options.C: 220 kWh per 1000 Gross Tonne Kilometres
options.D: 45 kWh per 1000 Gross Tonne Kilometres

e: Specific Energy Consumption equals energy consumed divided by Gross Tonne Kilometres, per 1000 GTKM. Here 88,000 / 40,00,000 x 1000 = 22 kWh per 1000 GTKM.

q: At an occupancy review, a division reports that against 95,00,000 seat kilometres offered during the period, its coaching services actually performed 57,00,000 passenger kilometres. The load factor (occupation ratio) reported for the coaching services is:
e: Load factor equals passenger kilometres divided by seat kilometres offered, as a percentage. Here 57,00,000 / 95,00,000 x 100 = 60 percent.

q: A finance officer is reviewing the annual results of a zonal railway whose gross earnings for the year are Rs 5,500 crore and whose working expenses are Rs 4,785 crore. The Operating Ratio of the railway for the year works out to:
e: Operating Ratio equals working expenses divided by gross earnings, as a percentage. Here Rs 4,785 crore / Rs 5,500 crore x 100 = 87 percent.

q: A statistics clerk is closing the monthly wagon performance return of a railway. During the month, the total wagon days on the railway were 12,60,000 and the number of wagons loaded was 3,15,000. The wagon turn-round for the month works out to:

options.A: 3.15 days
options.B: 3.0 days
options.C: 5.0 days
options.D: 4.0 days

e: Wagon turn-round equals total wagon days divided by number of wagons loaded. Here 12,60,000 / 3,15,000 = 4.0 days.

q: A costing officer has to work out the average lead of the goods traffic of a railway which performed 1,96,00,000 Net Tonne Kilometres during a period in which the tonnes carried were 2,45,000. The average lead of goods traffic of the railway works out to:

options.A: 80 km
options.B: 75 km
options.C: 90 km
options.D: 65 km

e: Average lead of goods traffic equals Net Tonne Kilometres divided by tonnes carried. Here 1,96,00,000 / 2,45,000 = 80 km.

q: A performance analyst has to work out the Net Tonne Kilometres per engine day of a railway which performed 71,50,000 Net Tonne Kilometres during a period in which the goods engine days numbered 1,430. The Net Tonne Kilometres per engine day work out to:
e: Net Tonne Kilometres per engine day equal Net Tonne Kilometres divided by goods engine days. Here 71,50,000 / 1,430 = 5,000.

q: A performance analyst has to work out the Net Tonne Kilometres per wagon day of a railway which performed 26,60,000 Net Tonne Kilometres during a period in which the wagon days numbered 70,000. The Net Tonne Kilometres per wagon day work out to:
e: Net Tonne Kilometres per wagon day equal Net Tonne Kilometres divided by wagon days. Here 26,60,000 / 70,000 = 38.

q: A traffic costing cell has worked out that the total cost of the goods services of a railway for a period is Rs 57,50,000 and the Net Tonne Kilometres performed are 11,50,000. The cost per Net Tonne Kilometre works out to:
e: Cost per Net Tonne Kilometre equals total cost of goods services divided by Net Tonne Kilometres. Here Rs 57,50,000 / 11,50,000 = Rs 5.00.

q: A traffic costing cell has worked out that the total cost of the coaching services of a railway for a period is Rs 91,00,000 and the passenger kilometres performed are 1,82,00,000. The cost per passenger kilometre works out to:
e: Cost per passenger kilometre equals total cost of coaching services divided by passenger kilometres. Here Rs 91,00,000 / 1,82,00,000 = Rs 0.50.

q: During a period, the total wagon kilometres run on a railway were 75,00,000, of which the empty wagon kilometres were 18,75,000. The percentage of empty wagon kilometres to total wagon kilometres is:
e: Percentage of empty wagon kilometres equals empty wagon kilometres divided by total wagon kilometres, as a percentage. Here 18,75,000 / 75,00,000 x 100 = 25 percent.

q: The passenger earnings of a railway for a period are Rs 1,76,00,000 and the number of passengers carried during the period is 22,00,000. The earnings per passenger of the railway for the period are:

options.B: Rs 6
options.C: Rs 80
options.D: Rs 8

e: Earnings per passenger equal passenger earnings divided by passengers carried. Here Rs 1,76,00,000 / 22,00,000 = Rs 8.

q: The gross earnings of a railway for a period are Rs 4,90,00,000. During the same period it performed 90,00,000 passenger kilometres and 50,00,000 Net Tonne Kilometres. The earnings per traffic unit of the railway work out to:
e: Earnings per traffic unit equal gross earnings divided by total traffic units. Here Rs 4,90,00,000 / (90,00,000 + 50,00,000) = Rs 4,90,00,000 / 1,40,00,000 = Rs 3.50.

q: A railway performed 88,00,000 passenger kilometres during a period in which the passenger train kilometres run were 16,000. The average number of passengers carried per train on the railway works out to:
e: Average passengers per train equal passenger kilometres divided by passenger train kilometres. Here 88,00,000 / 16,000 = 550.

q: The Net Tonne Kilometres performed on a railway are 5,60,00,000 and the loaded wagon kilometres are 16,00,000. The average load of a loaded wagon on the railway works out to:

options.A: 56 tonnes
options.B: 40 tonnes
options.C: 35 tonnes
options.D: 30 tonnes

e: Average load of a loaded wagon equals Net Tonne Kilometres divided by loaded wagon kilometres. Here 5,60,00,000 / 16,00,000 = 35 tonnes.

q: A loco foreman is checking a monthly return which shows that the locomotives of a railway ran 13,30,000 engine kilometres during the month and the engine days numbered 3,500. The engine kilometres per engine day work out to:
e: Engine kilometres per engine day equal engine kilometres divided by engine days. Here 13,30,000 / 3,500 = 380.

q: A statistics clerk has to report the density of passenger traffic on a railway which performed 1,90,00,000 passenger kilometres during a year in which the route kilometres open for traffic were 5,000. The density of passenger traffic on the railway works out to:

options.A: 38,000 passenger kilometres per route kilometre
options.B: 3,500 passenger kilometres per route kilometre
options.C: 380 passenger kilometres per route kilometre
options.D: 3,800 passenger kilometres per route kilometre

e: Density of passenger traffic equals passenger kilometres divided by route kilometres open. Here 1,90,00,000 / 5,000 = 3,800 passenger kilometres per route kilometre.

q: The goods earnings of a railway for a period are Rs 1,05,00,000 and the goods train kilometres run during the period are 1,50,000. The earnings per goods train kilometre work out to:

options.A: Rs 70
options.B: Rs 7
options.C: Rs 700
options.D: Rs 105

e: Earnings per goods train kilometre equal goods earnings divided by goods train kilometres. Here Rs 1,05,00,000 / 1,50,000 = Rs 70.
